def: Biot-Savart law gives the magnetic field dB produced at a point by a tiny current-carrying element Idl, and is the starting formula for finding magnetic fields of wires, loops and solenoids.
points: dB is proportional to the current I and the length of the small element dl.
dB is proportional to sin(theta), where theta is the angle between dl and the line to the point.
dB is inversely proportional to the square of the distance r from the element to the point.
The constant of proportionality is mu0/(4 pi), same role as k in Coulomb's law.
Direction of dB is perpendicular to the plane containing dl and r, given by the right-hand rule.
Total field from a long wire or loop is found by adding (integrating) dB from all elements.
formula: dB = (mu0 / 4 pi) x (I dl sin theta) / r^2

diagram.draw: Draw a small current element of length dl on a wire with current I marked by an arrow. Draw a line from the element to a point P at distance r, label the angle theta between dl and r. Show dB coming out of the page at P with a dot, using the right-hand rule.

example: Biot-Savart law is mainly used for derivation; it is combined by integration to get the field of a circular loop or straight wire (see next topics).
tip: Write the formula with all symbols defined, and mention it is the magnetic analogue of Coulomb's law — this comparison is often asked.

t: Magnetic field of a circular loop and straight wire
def: Using Biot-Savart's law, the magnetic field at the centre of a current loop and at a distance from a long straight wire can be calculated by integration.
points: For a circular loop of radius r carrying current I, the field at its centre is B = mu0 I / (2r), directed along the axis.
On the axis at distance x from the centre, the field is smaller: B = mu0 I r^2 / [2(r^2+x^2)^(3/2)].
For an infinitely long straight wire, the field at perpendicular distance r is B = mu0 I / (2 pi r).
Field lines around a straight wire form concentric circles, direction found by right-hand thumb rule.
Field increases with more current and decreases as you move farther from the wire or loop.
formula: Loop centre: B = mu0 I / (2r)     Straight wire: B = mu0 I / (2 pi r)

diagram.draw: Draw a circular loop carrying current I with field lines through the centre perpendicular to the loop plane, label B at centre. Separately draw a straight vertical wire with current I upward, draw concentric dashed circles around it showing field direction by right-hand thumb rule, label B at distance r.

example: A loop of radius 0.1 m carries 5 A. B at centre = (4 pi x 10^-7 x 5)/(2 x 0.1) = (6.28x10^-6 x 5)/0.2 ≈ 1.57 x 10^-5 T.
tip: Clearly separate the two formulas (loop vs wire) — students often mix them up in the exam.

def: Ampere's circuital law states that the line integral of magnetic field around any closed loop equals mu0 times the total current enclosed by that loop.
points: It is the magnetic analogue of Gauss's law in electrostatics.
Choose a closed path (Amperian loop) with symmetry matching the current distribution.
Sum of B.dl around the loop = mu0 x I_enclosed.
For a long solenoid with n turns per unit length and current I, the field inside is uniform: B = mu0 n I, and nearly zero outside.
For a toroid, the field inside the core is B = mu0 N I / (2 pi r).
This law makes it very easy to get the field for highly symmetric shapes, without doing Biot-Savart integration.
formula: Integral of B.dl = mu0 I_enclosed     Solenoid: B = mu0 n I

diagram.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A["Choose symmetric Amperian loop"] --> B["Apply integral of B dl = mu0 I enclosed"]
  B --> C["Solve for B"]
  C --> D["Solenoid: B = mu0 n I inside"]
  C --> E["Straight wire: B = mu0 I over 2 pi r"]

example: A solenoid has 1000 turns/m carrying 2 A. B = mu0 n I = 4 pi x 10^-7 x 1000 x 2 ≈ 2.51 x 10^-3 T.
tip: Show the derivation steps: state the law, choose the loop, then substitute — each step carries marks even if final answer is wrong.

t: Force on a current carrying conductor
def: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a mechanical force because of the force on the moving charges that make up the current.
points: The force on a straight conductor of length L carrying current I in field B is F = BIL sin(theta), where theta is the angle between current direction and B.
Maximum force occurs when the conductor is perpendicular to the field (theta = 90 degrees).
Direction of force is given by Fleming's left-hand rule or the right-hand slap rule.
Two parallel wires carrying current in the same direction attract each other; opposite directions repel.
This force between parallel currents is used to define the SI unit ampere.
This principle is the working basis of electric motors and moving-coil meters.
formula: F = B I L sin(theta)     (max F = BIL when theta = 90 degrees)

diagram.draw: Draw a straight conductor carrying current I horizontally. Draw magnetic field B lines going into the page using crosses. Show the resulting force F pointing upward using Fleming's left-hand rule, with fingers labelled Field, Current, Motion/Force.

example: A 0.5 m wire carries 4 A current perpendicular to a 0.2 T field. F = BIL = 0.2 x 4 x 0.5 = 0.4 N.
tip: Always mention Fleming's left-hand rule by name and show finger directions in your diagram for the direction mark.

def: A moving coil galvanometer is an instrument that detects and measures small electric currents using the deflecting torque on a current-carrying coil placed in a magnetic field.
points: The coil (N turns, area A) is suspended in a radial magnetic field B between permanent magnet poles.
Current I through the coil produces a deflecting torque, tau = N I A B.
A spring provides a restoring torque k*theta that opposes the deflection.
At equilibrium, N I A B = k theta, so deflection theta is directly proportional to current I.
This linear relationship, theta = (NAB/k) I, lets the scale be marked uniformly.
Sensitivity can be increased by increasing N, A, B, or decreasing spring constant k.

diagram.draw: Draw a rectangular coil of wire between the curved poles N and S of a permanent magnet. Show the coil connected to a pointer over a scale, and a spring providing restoring torque. Label the radial field lines pointing from N pole to coil to S pole.

example: If N=100, A=2x10^-4 m^2, B=0.1 T, k=10^-6 N m/rad, and I=1 mA, theta = (100 x 2e-4 x 0.1 / 1e-6) x 1e-3 = 2 rad (approx, for illustration).
tip: State that deflection is proportional to current (theta directly proportional to I) — this one line is often asked separately for 1 mark.

def: A sensitive galvanometer can be converted into an ammeter (to measure large currents) by adding a low shunt resistance in parallel, or into a voltmeter (to measure potential difference) by adding a high resistance in series.
points: Galvanometer has resistance G and gives full deflection for current Ig.
To make an ammeter of range I, connect shunt S in parallel so extra current bypasses the coil: S = Ig G / (I - Ig).
An ideal ammeter has very low resistance so it barely changes the circuit's current — hence shunt is small.
To make a voltmeter of range V, connect resistance R in series: R = (V/Ig) - G.
An ideal voltmeter has very high resistance so it draws negligible current from the circuit — hence R is large.
Ammeters are always connected in series in a circuit, voltmeters always in parallel.
formula: Shunt: S = Ig G / (I - Ig)     Series resistance: R = (V/Ig) - G

diagram.draw: Draw a galvanometer symbol with a shunt resistance S connected in parallel across it for the ammeter case. Separately draw the galvanometer with a high series resistance R connected in series for the voltmeter case. Label G, S, R clearly in both diagrams.

tip: Remember shunt (parallel, low R) is for ammeter; series resistance (high R) is for voltmeter — a common mix-up in exams.
